extracted.intended_audience: Employees of the United States Patent and Trademark Office (including career and political appointees, SES members, procurement officials, and attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Summary guidance on ethics rules that govern USPTO employees' conduct, covering general principles, misuse of government resources, gifts, conflicts of interest, outside employment, political activity, seeking employment, post‑employment restrictions, and financial disclosure requirements. Includes specific thresholds, permitted/prohibited examples, and filing timelines for disclosure forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Ethical Principle 1: Public service is a public trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Public service is a public trust, requiring employees to place loyalty to the Constitution, the laws and ethical principles above private gain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employees must familiarize themselves with Government ethics rules and comply with restrictions while performing duties and, in some cases, in personal activities off duty and after leaving service. Seek specific advice from an ethics official for application to particular situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Ethical Principle 2: No conflicting financial interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees shall not hold financial interests that conflict with the conscientious performance of duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle underlies disqualification requirements and thresholds described in the conflicts section.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Ethical Principle 3: No use of nonpublic information for private gain
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees shall not engage in financial transactions using nonpublic Government information or allow the improper use of such information to further any private interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to investments and trading based on nonpublic information obtained through Government employment.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Ethical Principle 4: Restrictions on soliciting/accepting gifts
rubrics_metrics.description: An employee shall not, except as permitted in ethics regulations, solicit or accept any gift or other item of monetary value from any person or entity seeking official action from, doing business with, or conducting activities regulated by the employee’s agency, or whose interests may be substantially affected by the performance or non-performance of the employee’s duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See detailed permitted/prohibited gift rules for categories (non-government donors, other Federal employees, agency gifts).

rubrics_metrics.name: General Ethical Principle 5: Honest effort in performance of duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees shall put forth honest effort in the performance of their duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General expectation of professional conduct and work product integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Ethical Principle 6: No unauthorized commitments
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees shall not knowingly make unauthorized commitments or promises of any kind purporting to bind the Government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid verbal or written promises that imply Government binding authority unless specifically authorized.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Ethical Principle 7: No use of public office for private gain
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees shall not use public office for private gain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes using government title, authority, nonpublic information, or resources to benefit oneself or others improperly.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Ethical Principle 8: Impartiality and no preferential treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees shall act impartially and not give preferential treatment to any private organization or individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid favoritism in decision making and recuse where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Ethical Principle 9: Protect and conserve Federal property
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees shall protect and conserve Federal property and shall not use it for other than authorized activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government equipment, supplies, services, titles, and nonpublic information are government property.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Ethical Principle 10: No outside employment that conflicts with duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees shall not engage in outside employment or activities, including seeking or negotiating for employment, that conflict with official Government duties and responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See non‑federal employment section for permitted/prohibited activities and approval/recusal requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Ethical Principle 11: Duty to disclose waste, fraud, abuse, corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees shall disclose waste, fraud, abuse, and corruption to appropriate authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report to OIG Hotline or other designated channels; Ethics Division does not investigate violations of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Ethical Principle 12: Satisfy obligations as citizens (financial obligations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees shall satisfy in good faith their obligations as citizens, including all just financial obligations, especially those—such as Federal, State, or local taxes—that are imposed by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain fiscal responsibility; failing to satisfy obligations may raise ethics or suitability issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Ethical Principle 13: Adhere to equal opportunity laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees shall adhere to all laws and regulations that provide equal opportunity for all Americans regardless of race, color, religion, sex, national origin, age, or handicap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comply with nondiscrimination laws and agency policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Ethical Principle 14: Avoid appearance of violating law or ethics standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees shall endeavor to avoid any actions creating the appearance that they are violating the law or the ethical standards set forth in ethics regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether an appearance exists is judged from the perspective of a reasonable person with knowledge of the relevant facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misuse of Government Resources — Basic Principle: Do Not Steal
rubrics_metrics.description: Government equipment, services, supplies, and other resources are paid for by the Government to promote public programs and must be used only for Government purposes or limited authorized personal purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even authority, nonpublic information, and Government title are public property and misuse may constitute theft or other violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted uses of government resources
rubrics_metrics.description: You may use access to the internet and a personal email account for personal research or to send a personal email; Government printers/copiers for personal purposes if not excessive; your Government title for personal purposes when not acting officially (e.g., biographical sketch) or when writing for scientific/technical publications with a disclaimer; frequent flier miles from Government travel for personal purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitted uses do not include business/profit-making purposes, political or lobbying activities, content that would bring discredit, discriminatory material, or uses that result in additional Government charges except where expressly allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited uses of government resources
rubrics_metrics.description: You may not use a Government credit card for personal purchases (unless specifically authorized); use Government computers/mobile devices to view sexually explicit material; conduct profit-making activities or run a business; engage in political/lobbying activities; engage in discriminatory conduct; use nonpublic information for personal purposes (e.g., investments); use Government time for personal activities; or use Government authority to assist on personal matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using your Government title for personal purposes is generally prohibited except limited situations noted under permitted uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal gifts from non-government sources — permitted conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: You may accept an unsolicited gift or invitation if it is offered by someone with no business before Commerce and not offered because of your Government position; from a relative or friend; $20 or less in value (and $50 or less from same source in year); invitation to widely-attended gathering with supervisor approval; a meal at which you are speaking in an official capacity; books/informational material ≤ $100 related to Commerce/profession (or >$100 with ethics approval); public discounts; offered because of spouse’s employment; small items (card/plaque); approved awards; certain business meals overseas; a meal/lodging/travel related to an outside business relationship; or gifts from a foreign government valued at $390 or less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain exceptions do not apply to political appointees when donor or host is a registered lobbying organization (with limited exceptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal gifts from non-government sources — prohibited conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: You may not accept a gift or invitation if it is offered by someone regulated by Commerce, has or seeks business with Commerce, or can be affected by performance of your duties (unless listed as permitted); if it is offered because of your Government position (unless permitted); or if it is specifically to induce you to take (or not take) Government action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even de minimis gifts may be barred if connected to your official role or from regulated parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal gifts from other Federal employees — permitted
rubrics_metrics.description: You may accept a gift or invitation from another Federal employee if it is not from a subordinate; $10 or less in value; for a special, major non-recurring event (birth/adoption, retirement, serious illness, wedding); food shared in the office; a gift of personal hospitality at the employee’s home; or a host/hostess gift.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may give a supervisor a gift only if it meets these permitted categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal gifts from other Federal employees — prohibited
rubrics_metrics.description: You may not accept a gift from a subordinate unless it is $10 or less, for a major life event, food shared in the office, or a host/hostess gift. You also cannot offer gifts to a supervisor except as permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protects against coercion or appearance of impropriety in supervisor-subordinate relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gifts to the United States Patent and Trademark Office — permitted
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO may accept a gift or donation of property or travel if it will further a Government program, is approved by the appropriate agency official, and acceptance will not create an appearance of loss of impartiality regarding agency programs or operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally means donor is not an agency contractor, grantee, licensee, or someone with interest in controversial matters before Commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gifts to the United States Patent and Trademark Office — prohibited
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO may not accept gifts that are of services (other than for travel); that will not further an agency mission; that create an appearance of undue influence (commonly barring gifts from agency contractors, grantees, licensees, or those with interests in controversial matters); or certain travel gifts if solicited or for first-class travel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptance requires approval and analysis of potential appearance issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicts of Interest — Financial conflicts: No conflict (permitted actions)
rubrics_metrics.description: You may work on matters affecting a financial interest in a stock or bond of $15,000 or less; in a broadly-diversified mutual fund; in a sector-specific fund of $50,000 or less; held by an adult child (if not living in your household); or interests covered by a conflict waiver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thresholds apply only to securities traded on a U.S. exchange unless otherwise noted; applies equally to spouse/household in certain rules with attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicts of Interest — Financial conflicts: Limited disqualification
rubrics_metrics.description: You may participate in general policy matters, but not matters involving specific parties, that will affect a company in which you hold stock valued at $15,001–$25,000; financial interests of a household member not spouse/minor child; or financial interests covered by a conflict waiver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial participation allowed for broad matters but recusal required for specific-party matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicts of Interest — Financial conflicts: Prohibited actions (disqualification required)
rubrics_metrics.description: You may not work on a matter if agency action will affect a company in which you hold stock greater than $15,000 (with certain higher thresholds for sector matters), stock totaling greater than $50,000 in companies affected by the matter, interests in sector-specific funds > $50,000, or financial interests not traded on a U.S. exchange (e.g., real estate, partnership holdings, foreign securities, stock options, patent rights), or entities with which you are employed, serve as officer, or serve on a governing board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribution includes spouse, minor child, household member, or general partner holdings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicts of Interest Based on Personal Relationships — permitted actions
rubrics_metrics.description: You may work on a matter involving a party (or its representative) with whom you have a personal relationship if the relationship concerns a former employer/client you worked for more than one year ago (career employees) or more than two years before appointment (political appointees); an organization in which you are a member but not active; or someone with whom your dealings are limited to routine consumer transactions; or if you have special authorization from the Ethics Law and Programs Division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special authorizations may allow participation despite closer relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicts of Interest Based on Personal Relationships — prohibited actions
rubrics_metrics.description: You may not work on a matter in which one of the parties is (or is represented by) someone with whom you have a business or financial relationship; a close relative; an organization in which you are active; the employer or client (or prospective employer or client) of your parent, spouse, or dependent child; someone with whom you were employed or served in certain roles during the past year; or (for political appointees) someone with whom you were employed or served in those roles during the two years before appointment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such relationships require disqualification to avoid appearance of partiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on investments and activities
rubrics_metrics.description: If a required disqualification would prevent you from performing important Government duties, you should not make the investment or engage in the activity. In addition, you may not use nonpublic information from Federal employment for an investment decision; if you file public financial disclosure (OGE Form 278), you may not invest in an IPO except as available to the public generally; and you may not obtain an interest in a patent (other than through inheritance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rules are proactive—avoid entering investments/activities that would create disqualification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-Federal Employment and Activities — permitted
rubrics_metrics.description: You may work for anyone who does not have matters before your office (unless otherwise prohibited); teach and write for pay if the subject is not related to Commerce programs/policies/operations; teach/write about Commerce if you do not disclose nonpublic information and are not paid (agency review or prior approval may be required in some cases); contact a Federal agency on behalf of certain family or beneficiaries with prior approval; practice law personally if not representing clients before a Federal agency/court or advising on matters where U.S. Government has an interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some roles (e.g., noncareer SES) have additional restrictions on pay for teaching/writing about Commerce subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-Federal Employment and Activities — prohibited
rubrics_metrics.description: You may not be employed by, or hold a position with, a foreign government; contact a Federal agency or court on behalf of someone else (with narrow exceptions); be employed by someone whose financial interests can be affected by your Federal duties unless duties can be reassigned; hold officer/board positions in organizations whose financial interests can be affected by your duties (unless reassignment possible); be paid for teaching/speaking/writing about Commerce programs/policies/operations except limited curricular exceptions; noncareer SES members have limits on outside income and fiduciary relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid roles creating divided loyalties or the appearance of using public office for private benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political Activities — permitted for all employees
rubrics_metrics.description: All employees may give funds to a candidate or party; attend political fundraisers/rallies; vote; sign petitions; display political bumper stickers on personal cars, wear political buttons when not on duty and not on Federal premises, put political signs on lawn; and run for office in non-partisan elections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitted partisan activity is limited by time/place/status restrictions (off duty, off premises).

rubrics_metrics.name: Political Activities — additional privileges for non-career employees
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees who are not career SES members may additionally assist in campaign management; serve as an officer in a political group; solicit votes (but not funds); stuff envelopes; and speak at a political event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-career status allows more active involvement subject to restrictions below.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political Activities — prohibited
rubrics_metrics.description: All employees may not engage in political activities while on Government premises or while on duty; use Government resources for political activities (including agency title, email, internet access); ask for or accept political contributions (with narrow union exception); host political fundraisers; use authority of Government position to support or oppose partisan candidates or parties; run as candidate in partisan election (with limited exceptions); ask for or accept volunteer services from a subordinate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Career SES members have further prohibitions: they may not assist campaigns even off duty or hold office in political organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seeking employment outside the Government — avoidance of participation
rubrics_metrics.description: You may not work as a Federal employee on any matter that would affect anyone you have contacted about possible future employment or who has contacted you about such employment, until you or the other party indicate the end of discussions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule prevents using office to benefit prospective employers during job discussions; act conservatively and recuse where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice requirements for certain employees regarding employment contacts
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are a member of the SES, a political appointee, SL/ST employee, or someone required to file OGE Form 278, you must notify an ethics official within three days of an employment contact that you will not participate in matters affecting the financial interests of the prospective employer. Procurement officials for procurements ≥ $150,000 must notify supervisor and ethics official about employment contacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely notice enables reassignment or recusals to avoid conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post‑employment restrictions on all employees — permitted activities after leaving
rubrics_metrics.description: After leaving Federal service you may engage in activities that do not entail representing others before the Federal Government; represent others on matters you did not participate in and which were not under your official responsibility during your last year (unless senior employee); represent others on matters that do not involve specific parties (unless senior employee); or represent District of Columbia or state/local governments before the Federal Government as an elected official.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitted activities still must avoid use/disclosure of nonpublic information and other prohibitions described below.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post‑employment restrictions on all employees — prohibited activities after leaving
rubrics_metrics.description: After leaving you may not represent others before a Federal agency or court regarding a specific-party matter on which you worked personally; represent others before a Federal agency or court within two years regarding a specific-party matter that was under your official responsibility during your last year; disclose or use nonpublic information (personal privacy, treaty negotiations, national security, trade secrets); or receive compensation for others' representational activities before the Federal Government during a period you worked for the Government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional restrictions apply for senior employees, political appointees, procurement officials, and attorneys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional post‑employment restrictions on senior employees
rubrics_metrics.description: Senior employees (base pay ≥ $161,755 or paid under Executive Schedule) in addition may represent institutions like universities or hospitals before their agency on matters that are not specific-party matters they worked on. Senior employees may not, for one year after leaving, represent others before USPTO (or entire Department for Exec Schedule employees); represent a foreign government before any U.S. Government branch; or assist/advise a foreign government regarding dealings with U.S. Government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senior status imposes more stringent cooling-off rules to avoid undue influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional post‑employment restrictions on political appointees
rubrics_metrics.description: Political appointees may, in addition to other permitted activities, represent institutions of higher education, hospitals, or medical research organizations before their agency on matters not specific-party matters they worked on. Political appointees may not, for five years, serve as a lobbyist before USPTO (or entire Department for Senate‑confirmed Presidential appointees); for remainder of President's term serve as a lobbyist before any political appointee in the Executive Branch; or engage in activity on behalf of a foreign government or political party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political appointees face longer and broader restrictions reflecting their senior policy roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional post‑employment restrictions on procurement officials and attorneys
rubrics_metrics.description: Procurement officials/program managers may not accept compensation from the contractor of a procurement of $10,000,000 or more within one year of working on the procurement. Attorneys must comply with bar rules which may prohibit certain behind-the-scenes legal services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procurement-specific cooling-off and attorney professional responsibility obligations apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial disclosure — OGE Form 450 requirements (procurement/public-affecting employees)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procurement officials and employees with duties that could affect the public may be designated as OGE Form 450 filers: file a new entrant Form 450 within 30 days of entering position and an annual Form 450 every year by February 15.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Your HR office can advise whether you must file; forms available at Ethics Law and Programs Division website.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial disclosure — OGE Form 278 requirements (senior officials, political appointees)
rubrics_metrics.description: Senior Executive Service members, political appointees, and SL/ST employees required to file OGE Form 278 must: file new entrant Form 278 within 30 days of appointment; file annual Form 278 by May 15; file termination Form 278 within 30 days after leaving Federal service; file a Transaction Report (OGE Form 278-T) within 30 days of a transaction regarding a security > $1,000; and file a Notice of Employment Negotiation within 3 business days of an employment contact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These public filings are used by ethics officials to identify and resolve conflicts; file via the Integrity electronic filing system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citations to applicable law and regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The summary references statutes and regulations that underpin the rules, including various U.S.C. sections and 5 C.F.R. provisions for misuse of government resources, gifts, conflicts, non-federal employment, political activities, seeking/post-employment restrictions, and financial disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult cited statutes/regulations and the Ethics Law and Programs Division for authoritative legal text and application to specific situations.
